h1: Sampling distribution of the sample proportion Calculator
summary: The Sampling distribution of the sample proportion calculator returns sample size (n) from the 5 fields on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. That makes it useful for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Sampling distribution of the sample proportion calculator work?
sections.html:
The Sampling distribution of the sample proportion calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports sample size (n) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the standard deviation of the sample proportion (σ_p).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Sampling distribution of the sample proportion calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Sample size (n)=population proportion (p) × (1 − population proportion (p)) ÷ (standard deviation of the sample proportion (σ_p) ^ 2)
Population proportion (p)=P_1 − standard deviation of the sample proportion (σ_p) × z-score of p_1
P_1=P_1
Confidence level=2 × (z-score of p_1) − 1
P(p p_1)=(1 ÷ 2 − 1 ÷ 2 × confidence level)
P(p < p_1)=(1 − (1 ÷ 2 − 1 ÷ 2 × confidence level))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Sampling distribution of the sample proportion calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the standard deviation of the sample proportion — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Sampling distribution of the sample proportion calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns sample size (n), derived from the standard deviation of the sample proportion. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Sampling distribution of the sample proportion calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the standard deviation of the sample proportion, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Sample size (n) = -0.9. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Sampling distribution of the sample proportion calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
